name: Adam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. Tell me what a normal workday looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I run a twelve-person purchasing operations team at a large home goods company. Each morning I check which suppliers missed a date, then sort the urgent orders with my leads and explain the bad news upstairs. I use AI every day to compare notes, draft a first email and spot odd figures, but I still check the purchase record myself. The part I enjoy is finding the one late component that holds up a whole range.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get that responsibility, and what do you have to fall back on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished an MBA, built a clear tracking system and took over when our old manager left. My title is senior but the pay hasn't caught up, and after rent, my MBA loan and helping my father with groceries, I have about three weeks of expenses saved. I live alone and there are only a couple of big employers nearby. I'm quick to try a tool, but I can't afford an unpaid experiment with my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the tools that save us five minutes and delete the ones that make more checking work. We still need someone to call a supplier when a promised delivery doesn't turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a little disappointing because I can see better ways to run this team, but my job would probably stay. My loan and my father's grocery money would still make payday feel very close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep my daily supplier list and let the AI draft only the first version of routine chasers. During the first year I'd cancel an unused streaming subscription and put the 12 a month into a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm about work because the purchasing problems remain. Money still nags at me, though; a flat tire would use most of those three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if that supplier chaser contains a wrong date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check it against the purchase order before it leaves my outbox. My name goes on the message, so the draft is never my excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job stays, but payday is close to the edge. Which feeling wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job feels steady; the household doesn't. My father's grocery bag weighs more than any clever supplier email.

say: I'd keep **small tools** that save time without adding checks.
A missing delivery still needs a **supplier call**.
think: My **role** probably stays, though better tools would be welcome.
The **loan and groceries** keep payday tight.
A **flat tire** could use most of my three weeks of savings.
do: Check **AI drafts** against purchase orders before sending routine chasers.
Cancel an unused **subscription** and save 12 a month.
feel: I feel **steady at work** but uneasy about household money.
S0.quote: My father's grocery bag weighs more than any clever supplier email.
fieldNote: He already uses AI daily but insists on **checking dates** himself.
His job remains steady while **family help** and debt drain savings.
He chooses a **small monthly transfer** rather than claiming a sudden financial fix.

steps.text: Continue checking supplier chasers against purchase orders before sending
Cancel an unused streaming subscription and transfer 12 monthly to emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team our purchase checks are exactly the kind of work the software will eat. I'd also say we can learn how to catch its errors and deal with the suppliers who don't fit the standard form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m fast with tools, but our director might decide one manager can oversee two teams once buying and checking are automated. I don’t want to prove that our purchasing team needs no manager and then receive the goodbye letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd build a trial on a copy of last month's 200 purchase orders and count false alerts before anyone changes the live workflow. In the first year I'd train the two team leads to investigate exceptions, ask my director for responsibility over supplier disputes, and send 40 a month to savings if my father is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, because I'm volunteering to shrink the routine work under my own job. The trial gives me a way to show what still needs judgment instead of merely saying it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the two leads when the trial starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them the false alerts, including the ones I missed. They should know the trial could change their jobs, and I would ask which supplier cases the software doesn't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run that test even if the director refused the dispute role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still run a small test because bad buying decisions cost everyone. I wouldn't roll it into live orders without a clear review job for the team.

say: Our **purchase checks** are exposed, and staff should learn to catch errors.
Supplier cases outside the form still need **human judgment**.
think: A director might merge **two teams** under one manager.
My trial could help remove **my role** if I have no next responsibility.
do: Test **200 old orders** for false alerts before changing live work.
Train two leads on **exceptions**, seek dispute responsibility and save 40 monthly if possible.
feel: I feel **anxious** while trying to shape the change.
S1.quote: I don’t want to prove that our purchasing team needs no manager and then receive the goodbye letter.
fieldNote: He treats **false alerts** as the test of the tool's value.
He openly sees that automation might remove **his own role**.
The savings transfer depends on continued **help for his father**.

steps.text: Test AI alerts on a copy of 200 past purchase orders
Transfer 40 monthly to savings when his father's groceries are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the company to set out who is responsible for a bad automated purchase, and what happens to the people whose jobs disappear. A fast rollout without names and dates would be reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My entire day is deciding and checking, so I expect my management job to go in 2028 or soon after. The robots around 2031 aren't my deadline; the thinking system is. Three weeks of savings won't carry my father and me through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight I'd list the loan, rent and what I give Dad, then stop the gym membership and put that money aside. Before 2028 I'd ask for the firm's redundancy terms and apply for a paid training place in electrical maintenance; after AGI arrives, I'd take an apprenticeship only if the wage covers rent and Dad's groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like learning new systems, but curiosity doesn't pay a deposit when income stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical maintenance rather than another office post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The building crews still need people for hands-on work until about 2031 in this picture. I'd ask a local contractor about vacancies and wages before betting my rent on it; I know robots could reach that work later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship pays too little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep applying for paid work and ask my father whether a smaller grocery transfer is possible for a while. I won't call an unpaid course a plan when rent is due on the first.

say: I’d demand clear **responsibility** for bad automated purchases.
The company must give staff **job dates and terms** before posts disappear.
think: Three weeks' savings cannot carry **two people** through a long search.
do: Cancel the **gym** and get written redundancy terms before 2028.
Ask about **paid maintenance training** and take an apprenticeship only if wages cover obligations.
feel: I feel **alarmed** despite liking new tools.
S2.quote: I won't call an unpaid course a plan when rent is due on the first.
fieldNote: He understands the **2028 thinking deadline** arrives before 2031 robots.
His willingness to retrain stops at the **rent floor**.
Support for his **father** makes a low-paid apprenticeship harder to take.

steps.text: Cancel the gym membership and place the fee in emergency savings
Apply for a paid electrical maintenance training place before 2028
Take a maintenance apprenticeship after 2028 only if its wage covers rent and father's groceries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to test automated buying in stages and pay people to learn something else. I would want the company to publish how many purchasing jobs it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a shot at clearing the loan and entering a paid trade program before my office job vanishes. It doesn't make me confident that maintenance will last forever, since the hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd attend the local technical college's evening workshop, practise basic wiring there and ask three employers what they pay trainees. I'd save 60 a month if Dad's needs allow, then seek a paid maintenance trainee position before 2031; in the first year after AGI, I'd stay in that position while checking how robots are changing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less trapped than in 2028. I would have time to try a workshop without walking away from my salary on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What answer from those employers would stop the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage below my rent and basic food would stop it. I'd keep my current job and look for another paid route rather than borrow for a course with no placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father think about your change of direction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He repaired lifts for years and thinks a real workshop teaches more than a glossy brochure. My father’s advice is useful; his grocery bill still has to fit the trainee wage.

say: I'd ask for **staged testing** and paid routes into other work.
The company should publish expected **purchasing posts**.
think: Five years could let me clear **debt** before leaving office work.
Maintenance may also change when **2034 robots** arrive.
do: Attend an **evening workshop** to practise wiring and ask three employers about trainee pay.
Save **60 monthly** if possible and seek a paid maintenance position before 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious** but have time to test a route.
S3.quote: My father’s advice is useful; his grocery bill still has to fit the trainee wage.
fieldNote: His father has **repair experience**, but Adam checks wages independently.
He distinguishes **2031 office risk** from later robot pressure on maintenance.
He will not borrow for training without a **paid placement**.

steps.text: Attend the technical college evening workshop and practise basic wiring this year
Transfer 60 monthly to savings when his father's groceries are covered
Apply for a paid maintenance trainee position before 2031 if wages cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use those years to make buying decisions traceable and give workers a share in the savings. A decade is long enough to show people the steps instead of handing them a surprise letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be excited to build a better purchasing system while I still have a team, and I could probably finish paying the MBA loan. But I wouldn't assume I'm still a manager in 2036; a good system could make my title unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a two-year project to record why buyers override supplier recommendations, with paid staff time to check every example and an agreed share of the savings before a tool learns from it. Starting this year I'd direct any pay rise first to the MBA loan and then to six months of expenses; before 2036 I'd move into a paid equipment training role if one opens, and after AGI arrives I'd keep teaching until the work or the 2039 robots change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the eventual job loss, but I can imagine steering the years instead of sprinting through them. Building something useful and leaving with savings feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would staff help record decisions if it might reduce their work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd need paid time and a clear share of the savings, not a speech about teamwork. I'd put those conditions in my proposal to the director.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait until 2036 to change roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd take a paid training vacancy earlier if the wage clears my bills. Ten years lets me leave by choice, before the office key stops opening a useful job.

say: I'd make buying decisions **traceable** and share savings with staff.
A decade allows **clear stages** before posts end.
think: I'd enjoy building the system while **my team** still exists.
The same good system could remove **my title** by 2036.
do: Propose a **two-year override record** with paid staff review and an agreed savings share.
Put any **pay rise** toward debt and savings, then seek a paid equipment training vacancy.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the end of the role, with room to plan.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me leave by choice, before the office key stops opening a useful job.
fieldNote: He sees a chance to **build the system** that may remove his title.
He asks for **paid staff time** and a share of savings before using their knowledge.
He would move only to a **paid vacancy** that clears his bills.

steps.text: Propose a buyer override system with paid staff review and an agreed savings share
Direct any pay rise first to the MBA loan and then to six months of savings
Apply for a paid equipment training vacancy before 2036 if its wage covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my office job could end before I can save even one full month. A written redundancy figure, paid training with a real wage and clear dates would help. I can learn quickly, but I can't make a missing paycheck by learning faster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether my team would be paid for teaching a system our purchasing habits. I'd rather build it with them than have their knowledge taken from quiet Tuesday mornings.

headlineQuote: I can learn quickly, but I can't make a missing paycheck by learning faster.
portrait: **Adam**, 27, leads purchasing operations and checks AI drafts against records every day.
His lower pay, MBA loan and help for **his father** leave about three weeks saved.
He tests tools on **old orders** before changing live buying.
He considers **paid maintenance training** as a route out, contingent on wages covering rent and groceries.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his thinking-heavy office job before he can save one month.
whatWouldHelp: Written **redundancy terms**, paid training with a viable wage and clear dates would help him move.
